dated.title: UTF-8 designed on a New Jersey diner placemat
dated.detail: Ken Thompson sketched the bit-packing over dinner with Rob Pike. Most websites now use what he worked out on that placemat.

dated.title: First .com domain ever registered
dated.detail: symbolics.com. A Lisp Machine company in Cambridge, Mass. The domain still resolves — bought by an investor who keeps it as a museum.

dated.title: Carmack open-sourced the Quake engine
dated.detail: Three years after release, the full source went up on id's FTP. Spawned a generation of engines.

undated.title: Karen Spärck Jones invented IDF in 1972
undated.detail: Inverse Document Frequency. It became a standard part of web search engines.

undated.title: grep is named after an ed command
undated.detail: g/re/p: global, regex, print. Ken Thompson already had it as a private tool, and made it public after Doug McIlroy asked for one.

undated.title: Radia Perlman wrote spanning tree as a poem
undated.detail: The original 1985 paper includes 'Algorhyme': twelve lines explaining the algorithm in verse.

undated.title: Alan Kay regretted the term 'objects'
undated.detail: He coined 'object-oriented', but said the big idea was messaging. Of 'objects', he wrote in 1998 that 'it gets many people to focus on the lesser idea.'

undated.title: Barbara Liskov built CLU on abstract data types
undated.detail: She's known for the substitution principle. She also led CLU in the 1970s: the first implemented language with built-in data abstraction. It had iterators and exceptions too.

undated.title: 'Computer' used to be a job title
undated.detail: From the late 1800s, often held by women. They computed ballistic tables, astronomical positions, census results: by hand. The machines took the name from the people they replaced.

undated.title: ENIAC was programmed by six uncredited women
undated.detail: Kathleen Antonelli, Jean Bartik, Frances Spence, Marlyn Meltzer, Ruth Teitelbaum, Frances Holberton. The 1946 press coverage left them out. Recognition came decades later.

undated.title: Women hand-wove Apollo's core rope memory
undated.detail: Each bit was a wire physically threaded through (or around) a tiny magnetic core. It got the nickname LOL memory, for Little Old Ladies. Errors were very hard to fix once woven.

undated.title: Margaret Hamilton popularized 'software engineering'
undated.detail: She led MIT's Apollo on-board flight software team, and used the term to get code taken as seriously as hardware. The famous photo of her beside a tower of printouts shows that code.

undated.title: Python is named after Monty Python
undated.detail: Not the snake. Guido was reading Monty Python scripts when he began implementing it. The community kept the in-jokes: 'spam', 'eggs' and 'parrot' all show up in the tutorial.

undated.title: Dijkstra wrote most later papers by hand
undated.detail: His numbered notes run up to EWD1318. He distributed them by photocopy and had no use for word processors. Over a thousand are online at UT Austin.

undated.title: PGP source code was published as a book
undated.detail: Phil Zimmermann printed the full source in a hardback so it could be exported. US crypto export laws had a loophole for printed books. MIT Press published it in 1995.

undated.title: First webcam was a coffee pot
undated.detail: Cambridge Computer Lab, 1991. Pointed at the Trojan Room coffee pot so researchers wouldn't trek to an empty one. Ran for 10 years. The pot is in a German museum.

undated.title: 1968 Mother of All Demos
undated.detail: Doug Engelbart, in 90 minutes, demoed the mouse, hypertext, video conferencing, real-time collaborative editing, and dynamic file linking.

undated.title: An early secure online purchase: a Sting CD
undated.detail: August 1994. NetMarket. Sting's Ten Summoner's Tales. The transaction used PGP for the credit card.

undated.title: AltaVista's Babelfish
undated.detail: Launched 1997. Free machine translation, named after the Hitchhiker's Guide creature. Grew to 13 languages. Yahoo killed it in 2012.

undated.title: Your terminal still speaks VT100
undated.detail: Released 1978 by DEC. Its cursor and clear-screen escape sequences are still in use. xterm and its kin are VT100 emulators with extras, like the colour the original never had.

undated.title: Yahoo started as a hand-curated list
undated.detail: Two Stanford grad students, 1994, manually adding new sites to a hierarchy of folders. Originally called 'Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web'. The directory survived until 2014.

undated.title: Plan 9 from Bell Labs
undated.detail: From the group that built Unix. Everything is a file: even network connections, even the window system. Never caught on. Named in homage to the Ed Wood film, and to make marketeers wince.

undated.title: The Story of Mel
undated.detail: 1983 Usenet post by Ed Nather about a programmer who timed his code to a spinning drum memory and wrote a loop with no exit test: it rewrote its own instruction until an overflow turned it into a jump.

undated.title: curl has had the same lead since 1996
undated.detail: Daniel Stenberg started it from a tiny tool called httpget. It runs in cars, satellites and on more than 100 operating systems. His rough estimate: 30 billion installations.

undated.title: BOFH has been running since 1992
undated.detail: Simon Travaglia's Bastard Operator From Hell started on Usenet, moved to The Register in 2000, still posts new instalments. Thirty-plus years of one sysadmin's revenge on management and users.

undated.title: RFC 1149: IP over avian carriers
undated.detail: April Fools' RFC from 1990 specifying how to carry IP packets by pigeon. In 2001 a Norwegian Linux user group actually implemented it: nine pings logged, four replies, 55% packet loss. They declared it a success.

undated.title: RFC 2324: the coffee pot protocol
undated.detail: April 1998. Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol. Defines a BREW method and adds the immortal status code 418 'I'm a teapot'. A Google Easter egg still returns it.

undated.title: Knuth pays for errors in hexadecimal dollars
undated.detail: The first to find an error in one of his books earns 0x$1.00: $2.56. He wrote real cheques until fraud stopped him in 2008, and few were cashed. Now it's a deposit at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe.

undated.title: 'lp0 on fire' is a real Linux error
undated.detail: The kernel's parallel printer driver uses it for errors it can't name: not out of paper, not off-line. Michael K. Johnson turned a joking code comment into the message in the 1990s. It's still in drivers/char/lp.c.

undated.title: Bechtolsheim wrote a cheque to a company that didn't exist
undated.detail: August 1998. $100,000 to 'Google Inc.' before incorporation. Page and Brin had to register the company to deposit it. Bechtolsheim had co-founded Sun in 1982.

undated.title: Anders Hejlsberg shaped four eras of programming
undated.detail: Wrote Turbo Pascal, out when he was 22. Then chief architect of Delphi, lead architect of C#, co-creator of TypeScript. Still ships code at Microsoft.

undated.title: Bram Moolenaar made Vim charityware
undated.detail: Bram Moolenaar led Vim until he died in 2023. He made it charityware in 1995: if you like it, help children in Uganda. Vim's start screen still says so. His charity, ICCF Holland, closed in 2025, and Kuwasha in Canada carries the work on.

undated.title: Fabrice Bellard's output is implausible
undated.detail: Wrote QEMU and TinyCC. Started FFmpeg. Co-wrote a JavaScript engine. Computed pi to a then-record 2.7 trillion digits, mostly on one desktop. Released LTE base station software.

undated.title: James Gosling wrote more than Java
undated.detail: Also: Gosling Emacs, an early Emacs for Unix; NeWS, a window system that lost to X11, as lead engineer; and, while still in high school, software to analyse ISIS-II satellite data for the University of Calgary.

undated.title: Wietse Venema wrote Postfix
undated.detail: Written at IBM Research, released 1998. An alternative to sendmail, built to be fast, easy to administer and secure. Venema also wrote TCP Wrapper and, with Dan Farmer, SATAN: an early network security scanner.

undated.title: Eric Allman started sendmail as a student
undated.detail: Berkeley, late 1970s. His delivermail bridged ARPANET, UUCP and the campus network, then grew into sendmail. By the late 1990s it ran most mail servers. He wrote it unpaid, next to his day job.

undated.title: Niklaus Wirth and Wirth's Law
undated.detail: Designed Pascal, Modula, Oberon, and two workstations: Lilith and Ceres. Wirth's Law, which he credited to Martin Reiser in 1995: 'Software is getting slower more rapidly than hardware becomes faster.'

undated.title: Lynn Conway rewrote how chips are designed
undated.detail: Co-authored the 1980 textbook that made VLSI design teachable. Earlier, IBM fired her for transitioning: she started again as a contract programmer and worked her way up to Xerox PARC.

undated.title: Paul Vixie looked after the internet's DNS software
undated.detail: Became the main maintainer of BIND, the DNS server born at Berkeley, and co-founded ISC to look after it. Also founded MAPS, a pioneering anti-spam nonprofit.

undated.title: Jon Postel was the RFC editor for 28 years
undated.detail: He edited the internet's RFC series until 1998. He coined the robustness principle: 'Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.' Quietly held the standards process together until his death at 55.

undated.title: Theo de Raadt and OpenSSH
undated.detail: He started OpenSSH in 1999 with fellow OpenBSD developers. It now ships with Linux, macOS and Windows. He still runs OpenBSD, with the same rigour. Both projects live on donations.

undated.title: JPEG 2000's wavelet is named after a Belgian
undated.detail: Its lossy mode uses the Cohen-Daubechies-Feauveau 9/7 wavelet. The middle name is Ingrid Daubechies, a mathematician from Houthalen. She later became the first woman to lead the International Mathematical Union.

undated.title: The Web had a Belgian champion
undated.detail: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first proposal alone in 1989. Robert Cailliau, a Belgian engineer at CERN, co-wrote the 1990 version asking for staff, and co-built the first browser for the Mac.

undated.title: The datagram came from a French network
undated.detail: Louis Pouzin built CYCLADES in 1973 and made the hosts responsible for reliable delivery, keeping the network itself simple. It's the principle TCP/IP was built on.

undated.title: A teaching OS ended up inside Intel PCs
undated.detail: Andrew Tanenbaum wrote MINIX as a teaching OS: the one Linus learned from. From 2015, Intel quietly put a version in the Management Engine of its PC chipsets. Tanenbaum found out from the press.

undated.title: Grace Hopper handed out nanoseconds
undated.detail: To show admirals why a satellite link lags, she gave them 30 cm wires — the distance light travels in a billionth of a second. A 300-metre coil was her microsecond. She also wrote an early compiler and coined the term 'compiler'.

undated.title: ELIZA's creator turned against it
undated.detail: Joseph Weizenbaum wrote it in 1966: a pattern-matching script imitating a therapist. People grew attached to a few hundred lines of code. His secretary asked him to leave the room while she used it. He later became an AI critic.

undated.title: AI was going to be a summer project
undated.detail: The 1955 proposal that coined 'artificial intelligence' asked for a 2-month, 10-man study at Dartmouth. McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon and Rochester expected to make a serious dent in machine intelligence over the summer of 1956.

undated.title: A critic of computer chess lost to a computer
undated.detail: Hubert Dreyfus's 1965 RAND paper noted that a 10-year-old novice had beaten a chess program. In 1967, MIT's Mac Hack VI beat Dreyfus.

undated.title: The first Black CS PhD built the tech behind Google Docs
undated.detail: Clarence Ellis earned his doctorate in 1969. In 1989 he and Simon Gibbs created operational transformation — the technique that lets many people edit one document at once.

undated.title: The .com/.edu/.gov scheme came from one team
undated.detail: Elizabeth Feinler ran the ARPANET's information center until 1989. Her group invented WHOIS and the top-level-domain naming still in use: .com, .edu, .gov, .org.

undated.title: Evelyn Berezin built secretaries a word processor
undated.detail: With management all but closed to women, she co-founded Redactron in 1969. In 1971 it shipped the Data Secretary: an early standalone computerised word processor.

undated.title: The first US woman with a CS PhD was a nun
undated.detail: Sister Mary Kenneth Keller earned it at Wisconsin in 1965, after a summer computing programme at Dartmouth. She went on to found Clarke's computer science department.

undated.title: She had a personal computer at home in 1965
undated.detail: Mary Allen Wilkes wrote LAP6, the operating system for the LINC, from her parents' living room in Baltimore. She later left computing to become a lawyer.

undated.title: SQLite is tested to aviation standards
undated.detail: It's on every iPhone and Android, and in the Airbus A350's flight software. Public domain, its core tested to 100% MC/DC: the bar for the most critical avionics code.
